The question of whether hot drinks cool you down in hot weather is genuinely contested, with conflicting research outcomes and expert opinions. Several sources, citing University of Ottawa research by Dr. Ollie Jay, argue that hot drinks can cool you down by triggering disproportionately increased sweating, whose evaporation more than offsets the heat added by the drink — but only under specific dry-heat conditions where sweat can fully evaporate [d1][d3][d4][d5]. A 2012 study published in Acta Physiologica similarly found that participants drinking the highest-temperature water while exercising had the lowest body heat storage [d6], and neuroscientist Peter McNaughton of the University of Cambridge supports the mechanism, noting that sweat evaporation acts as a coolant that more than compensates for the heat of the beverage [d10][d2]. However, directly contradicting this, a BBC-commissioned experiment at Nottingham Trent University found that a hot drink did not cool the subject any more than a cold drink, and a larger Australian study concluded that the body maintains core temperature at around 37°C regardless of drink temperature [d7]. The NHS, a high-credibility official health authority, explicitly advises people to avoid hot drinks during hot weather and instead opt for cold food and drinks [d9]. BBC Future acknowledges the debate is unresolved, noting that studies showing cold drinks are more effective may be methodologically flawed due to rectal thermometer placement near the stomach, but that hot drinks definitively fail to cool you in humid conditions or when sweat cannot evaporate [d11]. In summary, the evidence suggests hot drinks may offer a cooling advantage in dry-heat conditions via sweat evaporation, but this is disputed by experimental evidence and contradicted by official NHS guidance, leaving the question without a clear consensus answer.
